text: I write from the upstairs room of the inn, the route book open in front of me. You asked why we fell behind, so here are the reasons, in order. The track we intended to follow runs along an exposed ridge where the wind never lets up. It chills the skin and burns energy far faster than level ground, so we cut our pace right back. Then there was the previous day's rain. It had soaked the loose rock across the slope, and the stones rolled underfoot. Rather than force the narrow gorge, we worked our way around it. The longer line costs extra distance, but it removes any real danger of a fall. Accumulated tiredness cost us more time still, and we halted for a good while beside a capped spring. So expect us considerably later. The exact hour of our arrival will reach you tomorrow evening.

text: A reader writes to ask what can be done about the crowds wearing down the best known natural sites. The difficulty is one of clustering. Most visitors turn up in the same few places, in the same weeks, and the main path breaks apart under the traffic it carries. So what answers are there? The first is to spread walkers across the ground, marking out secondary loops that reach the same plateau from other flanks of the mountain. The second is booking ahead, which staggers arrivals and keeps the high shelters from being swamped. A third approach is to make the quiet months worth choosing, which means keeping the huts open and the shuttle service dependable. The last is a matter of teaching. Tell arriving walkers how thin the plant cover is, and far fewer of them wander off the marked line.

text: The guide kept saying the southern valley walks better than the northern one, and the mapmaker kept disagreeing, without once raising her voice. His case was simple. The southern path winds through soft grassland, it climbs at a steady angle, and it asks no skill of anyone. She granted him none of that. The far slope, she said, breaks into stony steps, yet it holds shade all day and water in quantity. He conceded the water, then came back to the heat, which drops as soon as the breeze rises late in the afternoon. A breeze comes and goes, she answered, while a wood shelters you without pause. They moved on to beds, a comfortable inn on one side, a bare hut on the other. In the end he said the choice belongs to the walker, and she agreed the two routes come out even, for opposite reasons.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Picture the old roads, long before anyone could survey a slope properly. You set out on hearsay and nothing else. Read the travel accounts left from those days and the same three worries come up again and again. Water first. Routes bent toward springs however far it took them, because a stage with nothing to drink cost you dearly. Then the ground itself. A wall of rock was worked around rather than climbed, unless the pass overhead cut whole days off the road. And last, a roof. People wrote down carefully where a traveler could sleep dry, and one lodging with a good name pulled all the traffic into some perfectly ordinary valley. Add the dread of fog, add the loose stone underfoot, and you get routes that look senseless drawn on paper and made plain sense to anyone hoping to stay alive.

units: a build-up of sand starts around a very slight obstacle

text: Where does a dune begin? With almost nothing. A tuft of grass, a pebble, a scrap of driftwood lying on flat sand. Wind carrying grains slows the moment it passes that small block, and what it carries drops out of the air. A bump forms. Every gust adds to it, and season after season the bump takes on a settled shape, sloping gently on the windward side and falling away sharply behind. Grains work their way up the gentle face, cross the crest, and slide down the back. That endless handover is what shifts the whole mass forward, step by patient step. Then plants take hold. Roots reach through the sand and pin it where it lies, and the wandering stops. What used to travel is now a fixed hill, one the breeze no longer redraws and walkers cross without leaving a lasting mark.

text: The boat began taking on water almost as soon as the cove fell behind them, and the whole journey turned on that. The current stood between the hull and the shore they had left, so they let it carry them, and it grounded them on a shingle beach no chart had bothered to record. Their provisions had swollen and split in the wet, and they abandoned them where they lay. With nothing left to eat, they had no choice but to climb the cliff in search of people. The ascent was long and dry, and it opened onto a level top of heather that the wind crossed as it pleased. From there they made out a pale roof below, and the wreck turned into a lucky detour. The farmer took them in for two nights and dried their belongings. One of them said afterward that a leaking hull had given him the widest view of his life.

units: the text speaks to whoever suffers in the shoulders from the first climb

text: Shoulders aching before the first climb is even over? Work through this. Tip the pack out completely onto level ground, then sort the contents into three piles, the indispensable, the useful, and whatever you packed from sheer habit. Discard that last pile without arguing with yourself. Weigh what remains. It should come to no more than a fifth of your own body weight. Pack the heavy items against your back, high, level with the shoulder blades, since weight sitting low drags you backward and ruins your footing on loose rock. Pull the hip belt tight before the shoulder straps, because the hips are meant to carry the bulk of the load. Then test the setting on a short slope you can run down. If a strap bites, let it out one notch and repeat the trial until the pressure feels even.

text: Two valleys that share a ridge have taken opposite views of how to receive walkers, and the difference is now written on the ground. The first spent its money on access, a widened road, a parking terrace cut into the hillside, steel footbridges thrown over the torrents. Visitor numbers there have doubled, shops have opened along the street, and residents describe a hum that never quite stops through the busy months. The second closed its road to cars at the last inhabited hamlet, so anyone going higher walks or takes the shuttle. Takings climb more slowly. Yet the riverbanks have stopped crumbling, and quiet has turned into a selling point. Officials from both valleys visit one another often, each watching the outcome he fears most. Neither has yet spoken of turning back.

text: The plateau opens out in steps, and no two of them look alike. At the foot lies grazing land, cut into squares by low hedges, with a path of pale sand threading between the pens and the drinking troughs. Higher up the heath begins. The soil turns dry, the growth stays low, and gray rock breaks through in patches. A wall of dry stone runs the length of the crest, on and on without a scrap of mortar, put there long ago to steer flocks toward the summer pasture. On the top nothing stops the wind, and the air carries a mineral smell, cold and faintly dusty. Two shallow pools hold the rain and draw birds passing through. On the far side a wooded slope falls away into a closed hollow, where a bench, a wooden shelter and a spring capped under a flagstone make a welcome place to halt.

units: the author considers that the way of traveling has gradually gone downhill

he asks only for a stop with no purpose, for the pleasure of breathing
text: Honestly, we have let travel slide, and it happened one step at a time. It used to be simple. You went out to walk. You followed a river, slept wherever the day ran out, and came home with aching legs and a couple of blurred pictures. Then the lists arrived, the places you absolutely must see, ranked and scored and ticked off in turn. After that a screen slid in between us and the ground beneath us, and we began looking at the pass through a lens before looking at it at all. Now you pass walkers hurtling down a glorious track with their eyes on their boots, desperate to reach a viewpoint chosen the night before. I want no golden age back, since those old wanderings were badly prepared as often as not. I want the right to halt for nothing whatever, out in the middle of nowhere, and breathe.
